entities.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) was the most visible leader of the American civil rights movement, whose non-violent resistance, soaring oratory, and moral courage dismantled legal segregation in the United States.

The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56) thrust the 26-year-old pastor into national leadership. Over the next decade, he led campaigns in Albany, Birmingham, and Selma, was jailed 29 times, and survived multiple assassination attempts. His 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' argued that injustice anywhere threatens justice everywhere.

His 'I Have a Dream' speech (August 28, 1963) at the Lincoln Memorial — before 250,000 people — is the greatest American speech of the 20th century. His leadership produced the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965).

He received the Nobel Peace Prize (1964) at age 35. Assassinated in Memphis on April 4, 1968, he became a martyr for human rights. The federal holiday on the third Monday of January honors his legacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Martin Luther King Jr.'s leadership and non-violent resistance led to the passage of landmark legislation, including the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965), resulting in significant social change and a major shift in American society.
